reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Timber Piles
sections.summary: Accessories protect pile toes and make splicing easier but add cost and should be used only when needed. Timber piles can split, broom, bow or break. Toe protection is a steel boot (no trimming) or a point (toe trimmed to fit). Heads are banded with heavy metal strapping; AASHTO (2010) requires collars or bands above 200 kips nominal driving resistance. Timber splices are undesirable: order longer piles or redesign with more piles.
sections.body: Chapter introduction (p. 395): accessories for toe protection and splicing are often cost effective with heavier loads, sloping rock, obstructions or long piles, but add significant cost and should not be used unless needed; they must develop the required structural resistance during driving and under all loads. 16.1 (p. 395): problems are toe and head splitting and brooming, body splitting or bowing, and breakage. 16.1.1 (pp. 395-396): larger hammers and higher resistances raise the damage risk at obstructions; boots cover the whole toe without trimming; points need the toe trimmed; both are secured quickly in the field by nailing the straps. 16.1.2 (p. 397): the American Wood Preservers Institute (Collin 2012 in the text; the reference list gives 2002) recommends banding heads with heavy metal strapping before driving; AASHTO (2010) requires collars, bands or other devices when the required nominal driving resistance exceeds 200 kips. 16.1.3 (p. 397): full bending strength of a spliced timber pile is virtually impossible to develop; AASHTO (2010) says timber piles should not be spliced unless the contract documents or the engineer in writing allow it; if lengths prove short, order longer piles or redesign with additional piles of the furnished length.
key_points: Accessories add significant cost; use them only when specifically needed
Timber toe protection: boots cover the whole toe without trimming; points need the toe trimmed
Heads banded with heavy metal strapping before driving (AWPI)
AASHTO (2010): collars or bands when required nominal driving resistance exceeds 200 kips
Timber pile splices are undesirable; full bending strength virtually impossible to develop
Short timber piles: order longer piles or redesign with additional piles

sections.title: Steel H-Piles
sections.summary: H-pile toes can deform and flanges separate from the web in fills, very dense gravel or boulders. Cast steel shoes (ASTM A148 Grade 90-60) prevent this and spread contact stress on hard or sloping rock; they are fillet welded along the outside of each flange, typically 5/16 in. or more. Welded plate toe reinforcement is not recommended. Splices are full penetration groove welds or manufactured splicers, chosen by the foundation loading and made by certified welders.
sections.body: 16.2 (p. 398): H-piles penetrate hard upper layers to dense or hard bearing such as rock, often with splices. 16.2.1 (pp. 398-400): non-displacement piles drive easily, but unprotected toes in man-made fills, very dense gravel or boulders may deform and the flanges separate from the web (Figure 16-4, found after dynamic test records showed toe damage). Manufactured shoes minimize this and spread localized contact stress on hard rock, particularly sloping rock. Plates welded to the flanges and web are not recommended: they give neither protection nor strength at the flange-to-web connection. Shoes are cast steel to ASTM A148/A148M (Grade 90-60), attached by fillet welds along the outside of each flange; flanges are usually beveled and a 5/16 in. or larger fillet weld used. Shoes from different manufacturers are equivalent if of similar strength materials and fabrication; minor shape differences matter little except where a shape gives a definite advantage. 16.2.2 (pp. 400-403): splices are full penetration groove welds along the web and both flanges or manufactured H-pile splicers, sometimes with a welded square or diamond backer plate. Splices must meet compression, tension and bending demands; the detail is set by the foundation loading. Strength beyond driving is needed for bending and cyclic loading, so certified welders follow approved procedures. Splicer method: notch the driven pile web, slip the splicer over, 5/16 in. vertical fillet welds about 2.5 to 4 in. long at its corners; chamfer the add-on flanges at 45 degrees, weld the upper corners the same way, then a full or partial penetration groove weld along both flanges. H-piles are typically ASTM A572 Grade 50 or higher, and splicers should be the same steel.
key_points: Unprotected H-pile toes in fills, very dense gravel or boulders deform; flanges can separate from the web
Shoes also spread contact stress on hard and sloping rock
Welded plate toe reinforcement not recommended: no protection at the flange-to-web connection
Shoes: cast steel ASTM A148/A148M Grade 90-60; fillet welded along outside flanges, typically 5/16 in. or more
Shoes from different manufacturers equivalent if similar materials and fabrication
Splices: full penetration groove weld on web and both flanges, or a manufactured splicer; detail set by loading
Splicer fillet welds 5/16 in., about 2.5 to 4 in. long; add-on flanges chamfered 45 degrees
H-piles typically ASTM A572 Grade 50 or higher; splicers of the same steel; certified welders

sections.title: Steel Pipe Piles
sections.summary: Closed end pipes usually get a flat closure plate 0.75 to 1.0 in. thick (18 in. diameter or less), 5/8 in. oversize for a 5/16 in. fillet weld; conical points cost more and flat plates give higher unit toe resistance; rock crusher shoes suit sloping rock. Open end pipes use cutting shoes; piles 36 in. or more use a thicker wall over the lower two diameters. Splices: full penetration welds on backing rings, preferred when full bending strength is needed, or friction splicers. Constrictor plates force plugging.
sections.body: 16.3 (p. 403): toe attachments limit toe damage and deflection; lengths are increased by welded or friction splices. 16.3.1 (pp. 403-408): closed end piles may deflect at obstructions and open end toes may deform in very dense material. Flat closure plates are 0.75 to 1.0 in. thick for 18 in. or smaller outside diameters (thicker for larger piles at the engineer's option), typically 5/8 in. larger in diameter for a 5/16 in. fillet weld, or the same diameter with a bevel and partial penetration weld; ASTM A36/A36M or better. Conical points (rounded or 60 degree) cost more, flat plates develop higher unit toe resistance, and a conical point may drive slightly longer for the same resistance; full or partial penetration groove weld; cast steel ASTM A148/A148M (Grade 90-60). A rock crusher shoe (thick plate with heavy plates forming a 45 degree point) is preferred on sloping bedrock. Open end cutting shoes (A148 Grade 90-60) have inside or outside flanges on a bearing ring; outside flanges ease drilling through the toe but enlarge the perimeter and can reduce shaft resistance, and are sometimes friction fit only. For open end piles 36 in. or larger, a thicker wall over the lower two diameters, with the same outside diameter, is the preferred protection. 16.3.2 (pp. 408-412): full penetration welds use a backing ring whose pins hold a root gap; friction (drive-fit) splicers, cast ASTM A27 (Grade 65-35) or A148 (Grade 90-60), are tapered with a 3/8 in. midpoint bearing; sections must be square (cut off damaged tops); without fillet welds to both sections full bending strength is not provided, the splicer must be fully seated before welding to avoid cracking, so full penetration welds are preferred for full bending strength; uplift suitability is the designer's call; spiral welded pipe often needs fillet welds to keep groundwater out. 16.3.3 (p. 413): constrictor plates welded inside large diameter open end piles force plugging at a target depth and a larger resistance (example: 60 in. pile); research is ongoing.
key_points: Closure plate 0.75 to 1.0 in. for 18 in. or smaller pipes; 5/8 in. oversize for a 5/16 in. fillet weld; A36 or better
Conical points cost more; flat plates give higher unit toe resistance; conical may drive slightly longer
Rock crusher shoe (45 degree point) preferred on sloping bedrock
Open end cutting shoes: A148 Grade 90-60; outside flange can reduce shaft resistance
Open end piles 36 in. or larger: thicker wall over the lower two diameters is the preferred toe protection
Full penetration weld on a backing ring preferred when full bending strength is required
Friction splicers: A27 or A148, 3/8 in. midpoint bearing; full bending strength only if fillet welded after full seating
Constrictor plates force plugging in large diameter open end piles; research ongoing

sections.title: Precast Concrete Piles
sections.summary: Concrete pile toe attachments are not routine; in hard driving or on rock a flat cast steel shoe or an Oslo (Rock Injector) point with a 3.5 in. hardened steel point is cast in, never added in the field. Embedded steel sections aid penetration. Prestressed pile ends are not effectively prestressed, so order full lengths. Splices are dowel, welded, mechanical or sleeve; Table 16-1 rates seven. A substitute splice needs field testing and equivalent strength.
sections.body: 16.4.1 (pp. 414-415): toes may be damaged in compression under hard driving; for hard driving and toe bearing on rock, cast steel attachments are added during casting, but they are not routine. A flat cast steel shoe or an Oslo or Rock Injector point (3.5 in. hardened steel point in a casting) lets the pile be chiseled into most rock; all attachments are fitted during casting, not in the field. An H-pile or pipe section cast into the toe aids penetration of very dense or hard materials rather than protecting the toe, sized for the concrete section, loads and soils. 16.4.2 (pp. 416-421): virtually all U.S. concrete piles are prestressed, but ends are not effectively prestressed within the development length, so order sufficient length. Splice types: dowel, welded, mechanical and sleeve (Figure 16-27). Table 16-1 (Mullins and Sen 2015): capacity means meeting flexural and tensile demands; ductile failure is preferable; durability is corrosion resistance; foreign made splices need special exceptions on some Federal funded projects; UF Tube is for voided piles. Epoxy dowel splices (holes cast or field drilled, dowels in the top section, sheet metal form, epoxy) resume driving after one to two days, are inexpensive but slow and have limited flexural and tensile strength. Welded (ICP) splices weld cast-in fittings around the perimeter. Mechanical splices (Kie-Lock, Herkules, ABB) use cast-in steel castings locked by bars, wedges, pins or keys; expensive but fast and designed for tension. The FDOT post-tensioned splice restores full prestress across the joint. Sleeve splices are fast and reduce tension driving stresses but cannot take static uplift; Hawaiian can sleeves need length and strength for lateral load; the short Bruns ring has limited tensile and flexural strength. A substitute for a specified splice should have equivalent strength and be field tested on spliced test piles.
key_points: Concrete pile toe attachments are not routine; used for hard driving or toe bearing on rock
Oslo or Rock Injector point: 3.5 in. hardened steel point; all attachments cast in, not added in the field
Cast-in H-pile or pipe toe sections aid penetration of very dense or hard materials
Prestressed pile ends are not effectively prestressed; order lengths that avoid splices
Splice types: dowel, welded, mechanical and sleeve; Table 16-1 rates seven systems
Ductile failure preferable to brittle; ICP and NU Chuck rated brittle
Epoxy dowel: driving resumes after 1 to 2 days; inexpensive but limited flexural and tensile strength
Sleeve splices reduce tension driving stresses but cannot be used where static uplift is required
Foreign made splices need special exceptions on some Federal funded projects
A substitute splice needs equivalent strength and field testing on spliced test piles

sections.title: Welded Splices and Toe Attachments
sections.summary: Weld quality governs pile strength. Failures trace to poor surface preparation, insufficient bevel or root opening, or ignoring approved procedures. H-pile add-on sections typically get a 45 degree bevel with a 1/8 or 1/4 in. root opening. Below 32 F ambient, preheat to at least 70 F within 3 in. of the weld and hold at least 50 F; no welding below 0 F. Shoes need a partial penetration groove weld along the full flange, not spot welds.
sections.body: 16.5 (pp. 422-423): Michigan DOT's Field Manual for Pile Welding (2012) and NYSDOT's Pile Driving Inspection Manual (2012, with minimum splice times by section and splice type) give guidance. A pipe splice cracked from bending during hammer-pile alignment; an H-pile splice welded cold without preheat broke a few blows later. Problems trace to poor surface preparation, insufficient bevel or root opening, or non-compliance with approved procedures. 16.5.1 (pp. 423-426): clean the joint and preheat below 32 F; without the bevel a full penetration groove weld is impossible; add-on H-pile sections typically have a 45 degree bevel and a 1/8 or 1/4 in. root opening; check alignment and root opening before welding with H-pile splicers (an extracted pile left its splicer and lower section in the ground). 16.5.2 (pp. 426-427): below 32 F ambient, preheat to a minimum of 70 F within 3 in. of the weld immediately before welding and hold at least 50 F until complete; no welding below 0 F. 16.5.3 (pp. 427-428): approved welders and procedures; spot welds on the web and flange corners can lose the shoe; a partial penetration groove weld along the full flange length greatly reduces that risk (Figure 16-43 is captioned full groove weld). 16.5.4 (pp. 429-430), Michigan DOT checklist: certified welders, an approved Weld Procedure Specification, joints per plans, ground and cleaned surfaces, preheat below 32 F and maintain 70 degrees (16.5.2 says 50 F minimum), no welding below 0 F, a quality control plan; electrodes in a sealed container or hot box at 250 F minimum, used within two hours of exposure or redried two hours at 500 degrees minimum, wet or dropped electrodes discarded; tack welds not part of the final weld; clean between passes; back gouge before welding the back side; final inspection for slag, size, arc strikes, cracks, porosity, undercut, underfill, overlap, penetration and fusion, with repairs before acceptance.
key_points: Welded splice problems: poor surface preparation, insufficient bevel or root opening, non-compliance with procedures
H-pile add-on section typically 45 degree bevel with 1/8 or 1/4 in. root opening for a full penetration weld
Check section alignment and root opening before welding when H-pile splicers are used
Below 32 F ambient: preheat to at least 70 F within 3 in. of the weld; hold at least 50 F until complete
No welding below 0 F ambient
Shoe attachment: partial penetration groove weld along the full flange length; spot welds can lose the shoe
Electrodes in a hot box at 250 F minimum; used within 2 hours or redried 2 hours at 500 degrees minimum
Tack welds not part of the final weld; back gouge full penetration welds before welding the back side
